extracted.intended_audience: general readers and historians interested in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and early 20th-century Canadian policing
extracted.subtask_description: A historical, narrative account of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (formerly Royal North-West Mounted Police) around 1920 focusing on duties, operations, patrols, organization changes, and traditions. Includes descriptive examples of patrols, legal authority, and institutional practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal status: national constable authority
rubrics_metrics.description: "Every member of the Force shall be a constable in every part of Canada for the purpose of carrying out the criminal and other laws of Canada and in the North-West Territories, and the Yukon Territory for carrying out any laws and ordinances in force therein."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section of the amendment of the Mounted Police Act quoted to show that members have authority across all of Canada; establishes legal jurisdiction and basis for federal enforcement actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty — enforcement where Canada is directly interested (Duty A)
rubrics_metrics.description: (A) "The enforcement, or assistance in enforcement, of all laws where the Government of Canada is directly interested or responsible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commissioner's summary itemizing primary federal enforcement responsibilities; guidance implies proactive enforcement or assistance when federal interests are implicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty — protection of public buildings (Duty B)
rubrics_metrics.description: (B) "The protection of public buildings of the Dominion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designated responsibility to guard government properties; part of the enumerated duties of the Force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty — protection of Navy yards (Duty C)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific duty to secure naval installations, reflecting national security responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty — Intelligence Service (Duty D)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintenance of intelligence functions within the Force; implies collection and use of information relevant to national security and law enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty — maintenance of law and order in territories and parks (Duty E)
rubrics_metrics.description: (E) "The maintenance of law and order in all territories and Dominion parks."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responsibility for public order across remote territories and federal parklands; underpins many described long-range patrols and outposts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty — maintenance of fingerprint bureaus (Duty F)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forensic/identification function included among Force duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty — paroled prisoners' record (Duty G)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative duty to maintain records related to parolees; part of broader supervision and record-keeping responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational principle — thorough investigation of remote crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Force follows up cases of murder, infanticide, and other serious crimes in remote regions "with the closest investigation even though it took months of work and patrolling amidst the rigours of Polar weather to do it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by multiple Arctic patrol examples; guidance emphasizes persistence, extended patrols, and personal hardship to secure evidence and enforce law regardless of remoteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational principle — protect legal rights of accused in frontier contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in remote prosecutions the Police ensure the accused "is deemed entitled to all the protection that British law affords," constituting courts (e.g., court at Chesterfield Inlet with a jury from the ship's crew) and bringing witnesses forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows commitment to due process: create appropriate tribunals, assemble juries and witnesses despite logistical challenges to preserve legal protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational practice — establishment of remote outposts and revenue/customs enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: New outposts were established in the far North (e.g., Port Burwell on the Hudson Straits to act for the Department of Customs and collect duties on foreign vessels; Tree River on Coronation Gulf for ordinary duty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational duty extended to customs enforcement and revenue collection in remote areas; demonstrates combining policing with fiscal/customs responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational principle — non-partisan neutrality in industrial disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Force "has never interfered in a partisan way when strikes and lock outs are abroad, but they stand by to preserve law and order and to prevent any destruction of human life and property".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline for conduct during labour unrest: avoid partisan intervention while protecting life and property; act as impartial enforcer of public order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational principle — independence from local influence and resistance to corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mounted Corps is described as "a force free from local influences... proof against all attempts at intimidation or bribery" which gives it unique effectiveness in cities and frontiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets an institutional standard of integrity and independence to ensure consistent, impartial enforcement nationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational duty — social-service collaboration at ports
rubrics_metrics.description: The Mounted Police engaged social-service workers (e.g., Rev. John Chisholm and Mrs. Bessie Egan) to meet unaccompanied women and girls landing in Canada, attend them on trains, and protect them from exploiters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates a preventive, protective role beyond law enforcement — coordination with social services to safeguard vulnerable newcomers at points of entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy — entry regulations for resource rush districts
rubrics_metrics.description: Superintendent G. L. Jennings and the Force "have made stringent regulations as to entry into the district" (Fort Norman oilfields) to protect the foolhardy from danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy tool to regulate access to hazardous/rapidly developing regions to reduce preventable harm; operational safety/regulatory standard rather than punitive enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personnel standard — promotion by recognition of merit and fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Promotions are described as coming "as a spontaneous recognition of merit" for men who "had won their spurs" and shown fitness and service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied human-resources criterion: advancement within the Force is based on demonstrated merit, service, and fitness for higher responsibility; accompanied by a list of promotions as examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rehabilitation/rehiring practice — use of reformed locals as helpers
rubrics_metrics.description: Convicted or pardoned local individuals (e.g., Sinnisiak) were taken back, sometimes appointed as special constables, guides or hunters, and used to instruct their people on the value of human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical policy of reintegration and leveraging local converts to influence community norms; used as a tool for moral education and local cooperation.
